segments.caption: A transformer cannot read text. It only computes with numbers.
segments.text: A transformer cannot read text. Everything it does is arithmetic on numbers, so the first job is to turn a sentence into numbers.

segments.caption: Step 1: the tokenizer splits the text into tokens.
segments.text: Step one. A tokenizer splits the sentence into tokens. Here each word is one token, but rare words are often split into smaller pieces.

segments.caption: Each token is replaced by its integer ID in a fixed vocabulary.
segments.text: Each token is then replaced by an integer ID, which is simply its index in a fixed vocabulary.

segments.caption: Step 2: each ID selects one row of the embedding matrix.
segments.text: Step two. Each ID selects one row of the embedding matrix. This matrix has one row for every entry in the vocabulary.

segments.caption: That row is a learned vector of 256 numbers: the token's embedding.
segments.text: That row is a learned vector of two hundred fifty-six numbers. It is called the token's embedding.

segments.caption: The sentence is now a 4 × 256 matrix.
segments.text: Doing this for all four tokens gives a matrix with four rows and two hundred fifty-six columns.

segments.caption: Step 3: add a positional encoding, because attention has no built-in sense of word order.
segments.text: Step three. Attention has no built-in sense of word order, so we add a positional encoding to each embedding. It tells the model where each token sits in the sentence.

segments.caption: This matrix is the input to the first encoder block.
segments.text: The result is the input to the first encoder block.

segments.caption: Start with one embedding vector per token.
segments.text: We start with one embedding vector for each token in the sentence.

segments.caption: Three learned projections turn each embedding into a query, a key, and a value.
segments.text: Three learned weight matrices project each embedding into three new vectors: a query, a key, and a value.

segments.caption: Query: what this token is looking for.  Key: what each token offers.  Value: what it passes on.
segments.text: Think of the query as what a token is looking for, the key as what each token offers, and the value as the information it will pass on.

segments.caption: Follow one token. The query of "My" is compared with the key of every token.
segments.text: Let's follow a single token, the word My. Its query is compared with the key of every token in the sentence, including its own.

segments.caption: Each comparison is a dot product: a large score means the key matches the query.
segments.text: Each comparison is a dot product, scaled by the square root of the dimension. A large score means that key is a good match for the query.

segments.caption: Softmax turns the four scores into attention weights that sum to 1.
segments.text: A softmax then turns the four scores into attention weights. They are all positive, and they sum to one.

segments.caption: The weights say how much of each token's value to take.
segments.text: The weights decide how much of each token's value vector to take.

segments.caption: The output for "My" is the weighted sum of the values: now it carries context from the whole sentence.
segments.text: The output for My is the weighted sum of all four value vectors. It is no longer just the word My. It now carries context from the whole sentence.

segments.caption: Repeat for every token to get the full attention matrix. Each row sums to 1.
segments.text: Repeating this for every token gives the full attention matrix. Each row belongs to one query, and each row sums to one.

segments.caption: All of it in one line: scores, softmax, weighted sum.
segments.text: The whole computation fits in one line: the softmax of Q times K transpose, divided by the square root of d, multiplied by V.

segments.caption: An encoder block takes the token matrix and refines it in four steps.
segments.text: An encoder block takes the matrix of token vectors and refines it in four steps.

segments.caption: 1. Multi-head attention: several attention heads run in parallel, each with its own Q, K, V projections.
segments.text: First, multi-head attention. Several attention heads run in parallel, and each has its own query, key, and value projections.

segments.caption: Each head can track a different relationship. Their outputs are concatenated.
segments.text: Each head can learn to track a different kind of relationship between tokens. Their outputs are concatenated.

segments.caption: 2. Add & Norm: the block's input is added back to the attention output, then normalized.
segments.text: Second, add and normalize. The input to the block is added back to the attention output, and the result is normalized.

segments.caption: This residual path keeps gradients flowing when many blocks are stacked.
segments.text: This skip connection, also called a residual connection, keeps gradients flowing when many blocks are stacked.

segments.caption: 3. Feed forward: a small network transforms each token's vector separately.
segments.text: Third, a feed-forward network. It transforms the vector of each token separately, using the same weights for every token.

segments.caption: 4. A second Add & Norm, again with a skip connection.
segments.text: Fourth, a second add and normalize step, again with a skip connection.

segments.caption: The output has the same shape as the input: one refined vector per token.
segments.text: The output has exactly the same shape as the input: one refined vector for each token.

segments.caption: Because shapes match, blocks stack. The original transformer used six.
segments.text: Because the shapes match, blocks can be stacked. The original transformer used six of them.

segments.caption: The encoder reads the whole input at once. Every token attends to every other token.
segments.text: The encoder reads the whole input sentence at once. Every token can attend to every other token, and the output is one vector per token.

segments.caption: The decoder writes the output one token at a time.
segments.text: The decoder works differently. It writes the output one token at a time.

segments.caption: Each predicted token is fed back in as the next decoder input.
segments.text: Each token it predicts is fed back in as the next input, so the decoder always conditions on what it has written so far.

segments.caption: Cross-attention: queries come from the decoder; keys and values come from the encoder output.
segments.text: The two halves are linked by cross-attention. Here the queries come from the decoder, while the keys and values come from the encoder output.

segments.caption: Problem: while training, the decoder could look ahead at the words it is supposed to predict.
segments.text: There is one problem. During training the full target sentence is available, so the decoder could simply look ahead at the words it is supposed to predict.

segments.caption: Masking: scores for future positions are set to −∞ before the softmax.
segments.text: The fix is masking. The scores for all future positions are set to negative infinity before the softmax.

segments.caption: Future positions get weight 0, so each token attends only to itself and earlier tokens.
segments.text: After the softmax those positions have a weight of zero, so each token attends only to itself and to earlier tokens.

segments.caption: Three families of transformer models follow from these two parts.
segments.text: Three families of models follow from these two parts. Encoder-only models such as BERT are used for understanding. Decoder-only models such as G P T are used for generation. Encoder-decoder models such as T five map one sequence to another.
